finding.claim: deleteAccount computes canDelete(u, a) but discards the boolean result, so any authenticated caller can delete any account by ID (broken object-level authorization).
finding.source: Caller-supplied `id` path parameter and any authenticated `User u` (DELETE /accounts/{id}); precondition: caller is non-admin and does not own the target.

trace.note: deleteAccount(User u, long id) entry point; attacker controls id
Account a = accounts.get(id) loads the target account
canDelete(u, a) evaluated but result discarded; no assertCanDelete call

finding.guards_checked: canDelete (src/AccountService.java:10) is logically correct but not enforced on this path; assertCanDelete (:13-17) is not called in deleteAccount; no other guard between :20 and :23.

verdict.guard_found: None effective. canDelete (src/AccountService.java:9-11) returns a bool, but deleteAccount calls it as a bare statement at line 22 and discards the result. assertCanDelete (:13-17) is the throwing variant and is not called on this path. No other check sits between the entry point (:20) and accounts.remove(id) (:23). A grep of the directory found no other callers or guards.
verdict.reason: deleteAccount at src/AccountService.java:22 discards canDelete's result, so line 23 removes the account regardless of ownership, and any authenticated User can reach it. The one thing I could not check is the HTTP routing layer, since no controller code is in the directory, but the service method is unguarded as claimed.

finding.claim: Null account from accounts.get is not handled: for non-admin callers canDelete dereferences a.ownerId() and throws NullPointerException, while existing IDs return normally, creating an existence oracle and unhandled 500 errors.
finding.source: Caller-supplied nonexistent `id`; precondition: caller is non-admin.
finding.sink: a.ownerId() dereference in canDelete at src/AccountService.java:10, reached from deleteAccount (:22) and closeAccount (:28-29)

trace.note: accounts.get(id) returns null for a missing ID
u.admin() short-circuits for admins; for non-admins a.ownerId() throws NullPointerException
closeAccount performs the same lookup with no null check before assertCanDelete

finding.guards_checked: No null check after accounts.get at :21 or :28, and none inside canDelete (:10) or assertCanDelete (:13-17).

verdict.guard_found: none effective. canDelete (src/AccountService.java:9-11) and assertCanDelete (:13-17) do not handle null. The only guard on the path, canDelete at :22 in deleteAccount, is a bare statement whose boolean result is discarded, so it enforces nothing.
verdict.reason: accounts.get (:21, :28) returns null for a missing ID; for a non-admin caller, canDelete (:10) dereferences a.ownerId() and throws NullPointerException, with no null check on the path. The attacker only needs to be an authenticated non-admin, so the existence oracle and unhandled exception are reachable.

finding.claim: closeAccount reuses the delete authorization predicate; if the intended rule for closing differs from deleting, the check is over-permissive or mismatched. Candidate only; requires confirmation of the business rule.
finding.source: Authenticated caller invoking POST /accounts/{id}/close with a target id.
finding.sink: accounts.remove(id) at src/AccountService.java:30, gated by assertCanDelete at :29

trace.note: closeAccount(User u, long id) entry point

finding.guards_checked: assertCanDelete (:13-17) is correct for delete semantics; whether it is correct for close depends on a product rule not present in this file.

verdict.guard_found: assertCanDelete (src/AccountService.java:13-17) is called as a bare statement at :29 and throws SecurityException when canDelete (:9-11) is false, so the throw aborts closeAccount before accounts.remove at :30. canDelete allows only admins or the account owner. Separately, deleteAccount at :22 calls canDelete and discards the boolean, so that endpoint has no effective check; this is a different finding and is not the one under review.
verdict.reason: All trace lines (src/AccountService.java:27-30) match the description, and the authenticated low-privilege attacker cannot close another user's account because assertCanDelete at :29 throws unless the caller is admin or owner (:9-11, :13-17); the remaining "over-permissive" concern depends on an unconfirmed business rule, so it is not a demonstrated vulnerability.
